item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating evidence-grounded explanations from plausible narratives. [FIRE (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05225) identifies inaccurate user-intent attribution, weak alignment with recommendation predictions, and repetitive explanations; its review-dependent implementation is unsuitable here, but its distinction between user opinion and recommendation reasoning is relevant. [Selective Generation (NeurIPS 2024)](https://proceedings.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/5a6815122f533193a022cbc41786c1cc-Abstract-Conference.html) uses textual entailment and human annotations to control unsupported outputs. These findings motivate an evidence-linked annotation protocol; they do not establish a validated recommendation-error taxonomy for this panel.\n\nA practical adaptation: annotate task-fit mismatch, explicit compatibility conflict, possible redundancy, and insufficient evidence separately. Each judgment should record the recommendation, relevant history IDs/timestamps, exact title/description evidence, and any explicit panel feedback. Compatibility conflict requires an expressed requirement plus contradictory item evidence; missing specifications mean unknown. Similar titles or repeated interactions can flag possible redundancy, but cannot establish ownership, lack of usefulness, or unwanted repetition. Immediate usefulness requires explicit panel feedback; histories alone provide only proxies. Validate these labels against the twenty users’ feedback, reporting per-category counts, annotation agreement, precision among assessable cases, and unknown/abstention rates separately. Treat this as exploratory diagnostic validation with a small panel; retain macro validation HR@10 for model selection and make no claims about unobserved diversity/conformity traits."}
